name: Like-Colored
opportunity: Sell US school and club basketball programmes a rules-legal BOTTOMS SYSTEM instead of a better game short: one colour standard expressed across a knee-clearing linerless game short, a colour-matched 3/4 and full-length compression tight, and a full-length game pant, all orderable together on a single roster order in the same team colour. The opening is a compliance fact, not a fashion one - NFHS Rule 3-4-5 requires uniform bottoms to be LIKE-COLOURED but permits teammates to wear multiple STYLES (shorts, skirts, pants), and FIBA permits compression undershorts provided every player on the team matches solid colour (A06-S3). That converts coverage, modesty and layering from per-athlete permission requests into an orderable stock SKU family, and it routes through the one channel in this evidence base that is bookings-led and low-markdown rather than promotional (A04-S9, A04-S1). HYPOTHESIS, not finding: nobody in this base has counted how many programmes would order a mixed set, and the rule has been open for three ordering cycles already without a brand response - which is either the whitespace or the answer.
target_consumer: PRIMARY BUYER (the person who actually orders): US high-school and club/AAU programme buyers - head coaches, athletic directors and booster treasurers placing roster orders through BSN Sports and peer team dealers, typically 12-20 units per order, once a season, against a compliance spec rather than a trend. The addressable roster base is real and countable: NFHS's 2024-25 participation survey records 540,704 boys and 356,240 girls playing high-school basketball, inside a record 8,260,891 total high-school participants (NFHS High School Athletics Participation Survey 2024-25, https://nfhs.org/stories/participation-in-high-school-sports-hits-record-high-with-sizable-increase-in-2024-25, published 2025-08; verified 2026-09-03). END WEARERS the rule was written for: girls' and women's programmes; coverage-first players (taller and longer-legged athletes); modest-dressing athletes who currently play in leggings under a short by permission; and the population already layering 3/4 compression under a game short (A06-S6, A05-S8). SECONDARY: Australian club and association programmes, where female participation is up 25% since 2022 to more than 450,000 women and girls and the league's on-court partner is not a performance-basketball brand (A02-S9). NOT the target: the individual retail shopper. This buyer's job is compliance and roster completeness, not self-expression - which is why it is a different opportunity from OPP-08 and OPP-03.
consumer_problem_jtbd: COACH / AD: 'Outfit my whole roster in bottoms that are legal, that match, and that arrive in one shipment - including the player who needs more coverage, the player who wears 3/4 tights every game, and the player who plays in leggings for religious reasons - without filing a permission request, without buying from three vendors, and without one athlete visibly not matching the rest of the team.' Today that order is either refused (everyone wears the same short and the athlete who needs something else opts out or plays uncomfortable), improvised (a black tight bought at retail that does not match the team's royal blue), or custom-sublimated by a small dealer at higher unit cost with minimum-order and lead-time penalties (verified: Hoops King sells fully sublimated custom compression tights in team colours at $41.99 each with an 8-unit minimum, https://hoopsking.com/products/mens-full-length-compression-tights, verified 2026-09-03). ATHLETE: 'Give me the bottom I actually need - more coverage, or a tight I am already wearing anyway - in my team's colour, that stays put when I am in a defensive stance, and that does not make me the one player who looks different.' Biomechanics is why the interface matters rather than being a styling note: basketball is the highest-lateral-movement team sport with up to 450 lateral movements and 42-56 jumps per game and an activity change every 2-4 seconds, so a short riding up in deep hip abduction or sliding on slick compression is a failure repeated hundreds of times per game, not once (A06-S1).
product_idea:
ONE COLOUR STANDARD, FOUR BOTTOMS, ONE ORDER FORM. The product is the colour library and the compliance spec; the garments are its expressions.

SILHOUETTES (all four available in every colour in the library, all four on one dealer order form):
1. ROSTER SHORT - linerless game short, knee-clearing across the full size grade. Inseams 7" (women's/youth block) and 9" (unisex/men's block), plus an 11" COVERAGE inseam flagged clearly as NFHS-legal but NOT FIBA-legal (FIBA requires shorts to end above the knee; NFHS regulates colour and logo but not length - A06-S3). No pockets: pockets belong to the free-play family (OPP-02/OPP-03), and their absence is a competition feature, not a cost-down.
2. ROSTER TIGHT 3/4 - below-knee compression tight in the same team colour, engineered as a uniform component rather than a base layer.
3. ROSTER TIGHT FULL - ankle-length compression tight, same colour standard.
4. ROSTER PANT - loose, straight-leg, ankle-length game bottom on the short's block, for coverage-first and modest-dressing athletes. This is the piece Rule 3-4-5 legalised and that no major brand appears to stock.

FABRIC: two platforms, one colour. Short body in recycled-content Dri-FIT knit at a GSM restored above the current Icon complaint band (A04-S6, A01-S3); tights and pant in an elastane-rich circular knit. The engineering problem - and the moat - is that these two constructions take dye differently, so the programme's binding spec is a shared colour standard with a stated tolerance (target dE <=1.0 between short and tight in the same colourway, measured on production fabric, not lab dips). If Nike cannot hold that tolerance the whole idea fails, because 'like-coloured' is a rule an official enforces by eye at the scorer's table.

CONSTRUCTION DETAILS:
- Linerless short with a soft internal waistband facing and a silicone or laser-textured internal grip band so the short does not slide over a slick tight (A06-S6, A06-S1).
- Gusseted crotch and articulated side seams, fit-validated in a defensive lateral stance and at jump-landing hip flexion rather than standing (A06-S1).
- Internal adjustable elastic waist plus a flat drawcord, so hip-first-graded women's sizes get waist control from webbing rather than from a cord that slips when saturated (A06-S9, A06-S2). Carried as a hypothesis to test, not a proven need.
- Single manufacturer's mark, sized and placed within NFHS logo limits, in an identical position on all four bottoms so a mixed roster reads as one uniform (A06-S3).
- Dimensional-stability and seam-strength spec written against a 20-wash protocol, because the reproducible consumer complaint on the incumbent franchise is seams and shrinkage after laundering, not pockets (A01-S3, A04-S6).

STORAGE: none on the competition family. Deliberate.

COLOURWAYS: a carryover stock library of roughly 12 team colours (black, white, university red, scarlet, navy, royal, purple, kelly, forest, maroon, vegas gold, orange, plus grey), every colour in every one of the four bottoms - not a seasonal palette. Black, white and beige are held permanently because NFHS permits tights in black, white, beige or the predominant jersey colour with all teammates matching (A06-S3).

NAMING DIRECTION: 'Like-Colored' is the internal programme name and should stay internal - it is the rule's language and it names the insight. Externally, host the family inside STANDARD ISSUE, which Nike already owns in basketball and which literally means 'what the whole roster gets': Standard Issue Roster Short / Roster Tight 3/4 / Roster Tight Full / Roster Pant, merchandised on one page as the ROSTER PACK. Avoid inventing a new franchise name for an architecture play - the buyer is a coach reading a dealer catalogue, and recognition beats novelty.
why_now:
The honest version of why-now is weaker than the synthesis claimed, and it is better to say so at the Council than to be corrected in it. THE RULE IS REAL BUT IT IS NOT NEW. I could not confirm NFHS Rule 3-4-5 as a 2025-26 change; two independent sources place it in the 2023-24 rules cycle, announced 15 May 2023 (NFHS Basketball Rules Changes 2023-24, https://nfhs.org/resources/sports/basketball-rules-changes-2023-24; KHSAA, '05/15/23 - NFHS Announces Basketball Playing Rule Changes', https://khsaa.org/05-15-23-nfhs-announces-basketball-playing-rule-changes/; both verified 2026-09-03). What WAS new for 2025-26 is Rule 3-5-6 on undershirt colour and Rule 3-4-4a on the school logo above the number - the 3-4-5 language appears in 2025-26 state summaries under 'New AND RECENT', which is almost certainly how it entered this evidence base as a current change. So the correct framing is not 'a rule just changed' but 'a rule changed three ordering cycles ago, the permission barrier it removed is gone, and no brand in this evidence base has built stock product against it.' That is a whitespace argument, and it carries its own risk: three seasons of silence may mean nobody wants the product.

What genuinely times this to SS28: (1) Nike's channel mix inverted - wholesale grew 6% to $27.5B while Nike Direct fell 6% to $17.7B, and Nike Digital has declined for ten consecutive quarters (A04-S1, A02-S7) - so a bookings-led dealer programme is aligned with where Nike's business is actually moving rather than against it. (2) The strongest first-party demand statement in the entire base is a retailer CEO's own call: Ed Stack said in Q1 2026 that 'the basketball business is coming back in a really big fashion and really built around the women's basketball business' and that 'boys and girls, young men and women are buying that product' (A04-S5). (3) Girls' participation is at record levels in the US survey cited above and up 25% since 2022 in Australia (A02-S9), and Nike's teen mindshare erosion is concentrated in girls (A01-S1) - this programme reaches that consumer through her coach, which is a cheaper route than brand marketing. (4) Team-dealer catalogues are locked 12-18 months ahead, so an SS28 bottoms system has to be specified now to make the book at all. (5) Competitors are retreating from performance basketball apparel - adidas basketball -21% in the quarter, Under Armour separating from Curry - freeing dealer shelf, though the freed space is small in absolute dollars.

key_features_benefits.feature: One certified colour standard across knit short, compression tight and woven-face pant, held to a stated dE tolerance on production fabric
key_features_benefits.benefit: Makes 'like-coloured' a purchasable spec instead of a coach's judgement call at the scorer's table. This is the entire product: without colour match across two different knit constructions, a mixed roster is a rules problem rather than an inclusion solution.

key_features_benefits.feature: Four bottoms - 7"/9"/11" linerless short, 3/4 tight, full tight, full-length pant - on one roster order form in one colour
key_features_benefits.benefit: Turns per-athlete accommodation into a line item. The coach orders a mixed set the way she orders a size run, and the athlete who needs coverage or is already wearing tights stops being the exception that requires a conversation.

key_features_benefits.feature: Linerless short with silicone/textured internal waistband grip
key_features_benefits.benefit: Deletes a component the layering player does not want (a hot, redundant brief liner over a tight) and fixes the failure it creates (a short sliding on slick compression) in the same move. The deleted liner is the densest fabric mass in a garment that traps up to 1.33 kg of sweat, and removing it funds the seam and dimensional-stability spec below. Caveat carried: players who do NOT layer still need a liner, so the lined short must remain in the line.

key_features_benefits.feature: Fit validated in a defensive lateral stance and at jump-landing hip flexion, with gusset and articulated side seams; hem certified to clear the knee across the full size grade
key_features_benefits.benefit: Basketball loads a short in deep hip abduction roughly 450 times a game with an activity change every 2-4 seconds, not in a running gait. A knee-clearing certification across every size is also the only way a coach can trust the 11" coverage option and the 9" long option are both legal for the athlete wearing them.

key_features_benefits.feature: Internal adjustable elastic waist plus flat drawcord on the women's/youth block
key_features_benefits.benefit: Women's bottoms are graded hip-first, which leaves the waist to a drawcord that slips when the garment is saturated. Webbing adjustment gives waist control that survives a full game. FLAGGED: the evidence for this is Nike's generic women's-bottoms sizing boilerplate, not fit or returns data - build it as a testable option, not a headline claim.

key_features_benefits.feature: Single manufacturer's mark in an identical position on all four bottoms, within NFHS logo limits, and no pockets on the competition family
key_features_benefits.benefit: Compliance is the product claim. A mixed roster reads as one uniform because the mark lands in the same place on every bottom, and the absence of pockets is what separates this family from the free-play family rather than being a cost saving.

key_features_benefits.feature: Seam-strength and dimensional-stability spec written to a 20-wash protocol, with the result printed on the dealer spec sheet
key_features_benefits.benefit: Team bottoms are washed after every practice and every game for a whole season by a manager, not by an owner. The reproducible complaint on Nike's volume basketball short is seams failing and shrinkage after laundering - a 3.9-star, 67%-recommend read across 64 reviews - and a wash-tested claim is the one durability proof a bookings buyer can actually use to justify a rebuy.

key_features_benefits.feature: Carryover stock colour library (~12 team colours, all four bottoms) rather than seasonal colourways, with a matching retail echo for individual replenishment
key_features_benefits.benefit: A programme buys the same colour for four years and replaces one lost tight mid-season. Carryover colour is what makes reorder possible and is the difference between a bookings franchise and a seasonal buy. The retail echo matters because a player who loses a tight cannot place a dealer order.

target_price.msrp: Team-dealer net per piece: Roster Short 7"/9" $32-38; Roster Short 11" coverage $34-40; Roster Tight 3/4 $30-36; Roster Tight Full $34-40; Roster Pant $38-45. Roster Pack (short + one tight, one colour) $60-70 net. Suggested retail on the parallel replenishment SKUs: Short $45-50; Tight 3/4 $40-45; Tight Full $45-50; Pant $55-60. NOTE: no price in this evidence base is anchored to a retrieved Nike price file; these are positions to test, not a recommendation.
target_price.tier: Core team / bookings tier. Deliberately NOT premium - this is a replenishable compliance franchise, not an innovation showcase, and every piece sits under $100 at retail.
target_price.rationale: Three anchors set the ceiling and the floor. CEILING: the incumbent solution for a colour-matched team tight today is custom sublimation from small dealers - Hoops King lists fully sublimated custom compression tights in team colours at $41.99 each with an 8-unit minimum (https://hoopsking.com/products/mens-full-length-compression-tights, verified 2026-09-03). A stock Nike tight at $30-36 net undercuts that on unit cost AND removes the minimum-order and artwork lead-time penalties, which is the real switching argument. FLOOR AND REFERENCE: Nike's own closest existing piece, the Pro Dri-FIT Men's 3/4-Length Tight, lists at $37 and street-prices $26.97-$32 (https://www.nike.com/t/pro-mens-dri-fit-3-4-length-fitness-tights-7tnCt4, verified 2026-09-03) - so a team-colour version at $40-45 retail is a modest premium for a colour-matched uniform component, not a new price tier. CHANNEL ANCHOR: BSN Sports lists a Nike Practice Short at $50 (https://www.bsnsports.com/c/apparel/shorts/basketball/, verified 2026-09-03 via search; page itself egress-blocked). NIKE LADDER CONTEXT: Nike's live men's basketball shorts ladder spans roughly $37 (DNA Academy 11") to $65 (DNA 6"), with the 10" discounting around 38% (A02-S4 counter-evidence); adidas' hero Crazy Lite short retails from $50 (A07-S10 counter-evidence). The pricing logic is deliberately NOT to earn a premium: Nike's June 2025 US price action exempted everything under $100, so there is no list-price relief on this ladder (A04-S8), and the margin case rests on the bookings channel's low markdown rate rather than on ticket. That is the whole commercial thesis and it is exactly the part the evidence does not yet prove.
target_price.regional_notes: US is the lead and the only market where the enabling rule exists - the programme is built on NFHS language and should be planned as a US programme first. AUSTRALIA is the strongest secondary on evidence quality: ~1.3M players, second among team participation sports, female participation +25% since 2022 past 450,000, NBL attendance above 1.2M, and an on-court league partner that is not a performance-basketball brand (A02-S9); price at AUD parity-plus-freight through Rebel/dealer, and verify FIBA-aligned Basketball Australia uniform rules before assuming the mixed-bottoms logic transfers. EUROPE: FIBA colour-match rules apply league-wide, but any recycled-content or performance claim on the spec sheet must clear the EU Empowering Consumers Directive, which applies from 27 September 2026 - three weeks after this analysis - and bans generic and uncertified environmental claims (A03-S5). FRANCE is a partial non-market for the modest-dress use case because the hijab is banned in federated play, which is a barrier rather than a demand signal (A05-S8). GREATER CHINA: no role in this opportunity. Nike GC fell 13% currency-neutral with apparel units -8%, Topsports stops selling Nike online by January 2027, and there is no equivalent enabling rule (A04-S2, A02-S2).

market_distribution_role: LEAD MARKET: United States, through Nike Team Sports into BSN Sports and peer team dealers - a bookings-led, low-markdown B2B pool whose orders are placed against a compliance spec rather than a promotional calendar (A04-S9). Australia second, through club/association programmes and Rebel/JD doors (A02-S9). CHANNEL MIX: roughly 80% team-dealer bookings / 20% a thin wholesale-and-DTC echo carrying the identical colour library, which exists for one reason - a player who loses a tight mid-season cannot place a dealer order, and a colour that cannot be replenished individually breaks the 'like-coloured' promise the programme is selling. Deliberately NOT an app-exclusive or drop-led programme: Nike Digital has declined for ten consecutive quarters while wholesale grew, and this consumer does not buy that way (A02-S7, A04-S1). ROLE IN LINE: architecture, not hero. It is a replenishable core franchise that anchors the COMPETITION family and gives the Uniform of Youth space a product with an actual order form behind it. It produces no image for a line review - that is precisely why it has not been proposed before, and the Council should be told that up front. It is the natural home for the residue of the rejected women's-category claims (waist control, coverage, extended sizes) because it delivers them as compliance rather than as a category argument (PAT-03, PAT-08). CADENCE: team-dealer catalogue cadence, with dealer books locked 12-18 months ahead of season and a carryover colour library rather than seasonal colourways - the opposite of the retail drop calendar. Success is measured in reorder rate and size-curve fill by door, not in sell-through weeks. RELATIONSHIP TO PORTFOLIO: distinct from OPP-03 (the men's core wholesale franchise and its make quality) and OPP-08 (a consumer-retail extended-size and long-inseam tier). It absorbs C-CONVERGENCE-2 (the linerless layer-ready short is this system's core garment) and the competition half of C-CONVERGENCE-1. It deliberately does NOT claim a women's category gap - A01-O2, A02-O2 and A05-O1 all did and all were rejected, and Nike ships 5", 6.5", 7" and 9" women's bottoms and put Aero-FIT on a women's signature short first.

evidence_stack.contribution: The enabling fact and the whole reason this opportunity exists: FIBA requires shorts to end above the knee and requires every player's arm and leg compression garments, undershirts and undershorts to be the same solid colour team-wide; NFHS Rule 3-4-5 requires uniform bottoms to be like-coloured while permitting teammates to wear multiple STYLES (shorts, skirts, pants) for religious or personal accommodation without a permission request; NFHS permits tights in black, white, beige or the predominant jersey colour with all teammates matching. Both legs surfaced through the skeptic's counter-evidence rather than the specialist's own research - the specialist used a Diocese of Cleveland PDF as an NFHS proxy. I independently re-verified the 3-4-5 language (NFHS 2023-24 rules-changes resource; KHSAA 05/15/23) and in doing so found the specialist's DATE wrong: the change is 2023-24, not 2025-26. The rule content is strong; the currency claim is not.

The engineering brief for the waistband and hem interface, and the best-evidenced signal in the entire base - it survived its skeptic untouched. Up to 450 lateral movements and 42-56 jumps per game, 31% of game actions lateral shuffling, activity changing every 2-4 seconds, confirmed against the Sports Medicine 2017 systematic review and independently corroborated by a 2022 MDPI Sports study of 140 professional and collegiate players. This is what makes 'test fit in a defensive stance, not standing' a spec rather than a preference. Narrowing caveats to carry: the review is 2017, '450' is an upper bound repeatedly restated as typical, and every dataset is elite competitive play.

The layering premise - 3/4 and full-length compression worn under game shorts, making the sewn-in liner redundant and the waistband interface a real failure point. This is the load-bearing consumer assumption of the tight SKUs and it is the weakest thing in the stack. The 'nearly every starter' claim traces to an annually re-dated SEO guide (2025 and 2026 versions of the same article exist); the only quantitative prevalence survey found (BMC Sports Sci Med Rehabil, n=512) reports 56.8% always/often in training and 72.9% in competition but is 88.1% endurance athletes with running dominant. The auditor reclassified this to HYPOTHESIS for the population that matters. Prevalence at high-school, club and college level - where this programme's entire volume sits - is not contested, it is unmeasured.

The human need for coverage-first and modest-dress bottoms: Griner on wanting to cover more leg, the Minnesota Muslim girls' team designing knee-length tunics and leggings, Basket Pour Toutes contesting France's hijab ban. Classified HYPOTHESIS and the auditor rated the need SUSTAINED but the evidence stale - the Griner quote is a May 2014 Mother Jones interview and the Minnesota project is the 2015 Asiya/Cedar-Riverside prototypes with hijabs launched commercially in 2017. Its whitespace claim is contradicted twice (Asiya has sold modest basketball components for a decade; Nike already ships an 11" DNA Academy marketed for extra coverage and a 9" women's option). What survives, and what this opportunity uses, is narrower: there is no purpose-built, integrated, TEAM-COLOUR-MATCHED bottoms system carrying a major-brand performance spec and an orderable dealer SKU. The auditor's own recommendation was to replace this signal's evidence with the NFHS rule - which is exactly what this opportunity does.

The channel thesis: team-dealer/uniform is a bookings-led, low-markdown B2B pool that Nike reaches through BSN Sports, growing with participation regardless of mall promotions; Varsity revenue and EBITDA up ~8% and ~10% in 2025. This is the commercial half of the whole idea and it is thinly evidenced. The auditor downgraded it: the signal contains NO basketball-shorts data of any kind, the revenue base is contradicted (Moody's ~$2.7B for the twelve months to September 2025 against the $2.3B youth-sports-blog estimate), an unresolved $633M BSN discrepancy sits in the file, and neither the $75M club/select figure nor the $5B segment size could be corroborated anywhere. Only the Varsity growth figures survive intact - and Varsity is consolidating under a KKR-backed buyer, which changes Nike's negotiating position rather than simply opening a pool.

The demand call-out that reaches the end wearer: Ed Stack on the Q1 2026 Dick's call saying 'the basketball business is coming back in a really big fashion and really built around the women's basketball business, whether that's Sabrina, A'ja Wilson' and that 'boys and girls, young men and women are buying that product'. That is a senior, first-party, on-the-record retailer statement and it is stronger than the numbers it was originally attached to - the +233% and +601% figures must be struck, being the WNBA's own 2024 season-review release laundered through an AI aggregator and mis-dated. Note what the quote actually says: CROSS-GENDER demand, which is a better fit for a like-coloured roster system than for a women's-only programme.

Why a bookings-led programme is aligned rather than contrarian: FY26 wholesale $27.5B up 6% against Nike Direct $17.7B down 6%; Performance grew mid-single digits led by Running, Football and Basketball while Sportswear and Jordan streetwear stalled; apparel +4% currency-neutral with units +2%. Every figure independently reproduced. The caveat that must travel with it: Nike does not disclose basketball apparel separately and the visible basketball momentum is footwear-weighted (Kobe alone ~37% of signature basketball shoe sales on StockX), so 'basketball grew' cannot by itself carry an apparel bet.

Independent confirmation that the channel logic holds beyond Nike's own framing: Nike Digital down for a tenth consecutive quarter (-12% in Q4 FY26) while wholesale grew 4% for both Q4 and the full year, and New Balance's growth is door-led (80 new doors, owned retail past $1B). Supports building this for replenishable sell-through with a clear ladder rather than as an app-exclusive drop. Honest caveat the skeptic raised: Nike's wholesale swing is substantially a deliberate strategy under a new CEO, not necessarily an industry-wide structural shift.

The secondary market, and the best-verified non-US signal in the entire base - every skeptic correction ran in its favour. ~1.3M Australian players, second among team participation sports nationally, female participation +25% since 2022 to more than 450,000 women and girls via the She Hoops programme, an estimated 150,000 players turned away for lack of court space, NBL 2025-26 attendance of 1,231,796 (+9%, 6,908 average, 63 sellouts, third consecutive million-plus season), and Champion confirmed as on-court partner through NBL26 - a league apparel partner that is not a performance-basketball leader. This is the one geography where a female-participation tailwind is measured by a national registry rather than inferred from a US league's marketing.

The waist-control and wet-state detail. Nike's guidance to order women's bottoms by hip measurement implies waist slack absorbed by a drawcord; sweat data supplies the reason that matters - basketball uniforms trap 0.00-1.33 kg of sweat (Baker 2017, Physiological Reports), a wider range than treadmill running, so the drawcord is asked to hold a saturated garment. The auditor stripped A06-S9's FACT classification: the hip-first sentence is Nike's generic women's-bottoms boilerplate, identical on the general Women's Bottoms and Women's Numeric charts and standard across the industry, and the chain from it to 'the waist is under-fitted' to 'an adjustable waistband is the answer' has no evidence at any link. A06-S2's own normative correction also matters: basketball's whole-body sweating rate is 0.95 +/- 0.42 L/h, near the bottom of team sports, so specify to the trapped-sweat garment number rather than to a near-worst-case rate.

Why reaching the girls' programme through her coach is worth doing: Piper Sandler spring 2025 (n=6,455) shows a 13-point year-on-year drop in Nike mindshare among female teens, with female share under 40% for the first time since 2020, and fall-2025 coverage attributes the 'stabilisation' specifically to the MALE upper-income bracket while stating share among girls is still declining. Two corrections that must travel: the headline 49% is Nike's FOOTWEAR mindshare - apparel mindshare is 26% (Hollister 12%, Brandy Melville 6%) - and the spring 2026 survey exists and was not consulted. This is a US-only teen survey.

The construction and price precedent for a women's-graded block inside this system: Sabrina's woven-front/knit-back hybrid with side pockets and snap cargo at $65 with a plus-size SKU (FB8427), plus the concrete, actionable defect that the reversible version has pockets on only one side. Establishes that women's-specific construction earns a price in this category. Counterweight the skeptic found: reviewers report wearing Sabrina at home more than for basketball, so the $65 willingness-to-pay is partly lifestyle-driven, and a women's 5" Crossover already exists at $65 - so 'women have no length choice' is false.

contradictory_evidence.description: THE WHY-NOW IS WRONG AS WRITTEN, AND I FOUND IT MYSELF. The synthesis presents NFHS Rule 3-4-5 (like-coloured bottoms, multiple styles permitted) as a 2025-26 change and builds the entire timing argument on it. Two independent sources place it in the 2023-24 cycle, announced 15 May 2023 (NFHS Basketball Rules Changes 2023-24, https://nfhs.org/resources/sports/basketball-rules-changes-2023-24; KHSAA, https://khsaa.org/05-15-23-nfhs-announces-basketball-playing-rule-changes/, both verified 2026-09-03). The genuinely new 2025-26 uniform items are Rule 3-5-6 (undershirt colour under visiting jerseys) and Rule 3-4-4a (school logo above the number); 3-4-5 appears in 2025-26 state summaries under 'New AND RECENT', which is the most likely path by which it entered this evidence base as current. Consequence: the opening has been available for three ordering cycles with no evident stock product from any brand. That is either the whitespace or the market's answer, and the Council must be given both readings. It also removes the urgency argument entirely - this can be planned properly rather than rushed.

The layering prevalence that justifies the tight SKUs and the linerless short is UNMEASURED in the exact population this programme sells to. The 'near-universal at elite level' claim comes from an annually re-dated SEO guide; the only real prevalence survey (BMC, n=512) is 88.1% endurance athletes with running dominant, 56.8% always/often in training and 72.9% in competition, and re-injury prevention rather than warmth as the leading motivation. The auditor's verdict on durability was 'unclear'. No basketball-specific figure exists at high-school, club or college level anywhere in the reachable literature. If sub-elite layering prevalence is low, the 3/4 and full tight SKUs have no roster demand and the system collapses to a short.

The channel signal contains no basketball-shorts data of any kind, yet the entire commercial case rests on it. The auditor downgraded it: revenue base contradicted (Moody's ~$2.7B twelve months to September 2025 vs the $2.3B youth-sports-blog figure the file uses), an unresolved $633M BSN discrepancy left in the file, and neither the $75M club/select figure nor the $5B segment size corroborable in any source. Additionally, Varsity Brands is consolidating under a KKR-backed buyer and is acquiring a soccer apparel company serving premier youth clubs - the channel is concentrating around a single counterparty, which changes Nike's negotiating position rather than simply opening a pool. Nobody has counted a single basketball-shorts unit through this channel.

CORE youth participation - the thing a team-dealer programme is actually sized off - is contested, and the audit explicitly warns against merging it with casual participation. SFIA and Project Play, the methodologically documented US datasets, report flag football as the only team sport with growth in REGULAR participation among children aged 6-17 between 2019 and 2024, with basketball's post-Paris lift around 7% and concentrated in CASUAL participation; Sport England Active Lives 2024-25 records a significant 1% DECREASE in weekly under-16 basketball players in England. Set against that: the NFHS 2024-25 survey I verified shows record overall high-school participation with 540,704 boys and 356,240 girls in basketball. Roster counts are healthy in the US school channel; whether the addressable base is GROWING is not established, and the club/AAU half of the target is not measured at all.

The coverage-and-modesty whitespace is contradicted from two directions. Asiya has sold modest basketball components - knee-length tunics and matching leggings, sport hijabs at $30-40 - for roughly a decade (prototypes 2015, hijabs commercial 2017; https://www.refinery29.com/en-us/2016/11/131222/asiya-sports-hijabs-modest-sportswear, verified 2026-09-03), so the category has an incumbent with ten years of product. And Nike itself already ships an 11" DNA Academy short marketed for extra coverage plus a 9" women's option, so the coverage LENGTH is not missing from the line - it is merely the line's cheapest, least-graded product (PAT-08). What remains genuinely open is narrower than the opportunity's framing: a colour-matched, team-orderable system, not a coverage garment. Separately, France bans the hijab in federated play, which makes it a barrier to the opportunity rather than a market for it.

The FIBA 'compression undershorts legal at ANY length' leg needs a primary read before it enters a spec sheet. My own verification surfaced the 'may be worn with any length' language attached to the compression UNDERSHIRT (on and below the shoulders up to the bottom of the neck), not unambiguously to undershorts, and I could not retrieve the FIBA rules or Official Interpretations PDFs directly - assets.fiba.basketball is egress-blocked from this environment. What IS solidly confirmed is the team-wide same-solid-colour requirement for all arm and leg compression garments including undershirts and undershorts, and that shorts must end above the knee. The colour-match half - which is what this opportunity actually sells - is safe. The length half is not yet verified and must be read from the current FIBA rulebook before any 'FIBA-legal at any length' claim is printed.

The waist-control feature rests on a sentence that says nothing about basketball. 'If your body measurements for hips and waist correspond to different sizes, order according to your hip measurement' is Nike's generic women's-bottoms boilerplate, identical on the Women's Bottoms and Women's Numeric charts and standard industry practice. The specialist itself conceded it found no quantitative women's fit-complaint data. The auditor removed the FACT classification. Treat the internal adjustable waist as an option to test in a fit study, never as a headline benefit.

The 'low-markdown channel' claim is asserted, not measured, and it sits next to a general promotional read that is itself contested. Ed Stack's 'increasingly promotional' quote was attributed by Stack himself to Foot Locker's exposure to legacy footwear silhouettes and launch/retro product, while the Dick's banner delivered +4.9% comps with broad-based growth including apparel - and Foot Locker US comps were +6% in Q1 2026 before -3.6% in Q2. The auditor's resolution is the important one for this opportunity: neither the pessimistic nor the optimistic read is about basketball shorts, because nobody has looked at basketball shorts. Nike's own markdown rate on team-channel basketball bottoms is unknown to this analysis.

Deleting the liner - proposed here as the funding mechanism for the seam and wash spec - has no consumer evidence behind it and creates a new problem. Players who do NOT layer still need a liner or gusset, and hot-market outdoor players especially so. The linerless short must therefore be an ADDITIONAL SKU, not a replacement, which removes the cost saving that was supposed to fund the make improvement and adds SKU count to a programme whose whole argument is order-form simplicity. This is the single most likely place the P&L breaks.

The demand evidence pointing at girls' programmes is directionally consistent but individually damaged. A01-S1's headline 49% is Nike's FOOTWEAR mindshare, not apparel (apparel is 26%), and the fall-2025 'stabilisation' applies to male upper-income teens while girls' share is still declining - a correction that strengthens the strategic implication but falsifies the finding as written. A04-S5's quantified half (+233% at Dick's, +601% at WNBAStore) is the WNBA's own 2024 season-review release measured against a pre-Caitlin-Clark 2023 base, laundered through an AI aggregator and mis-dated to 2025; those numbers must not be repeated. What survives is Stack's own words and a US teen survey with a metric error - enough to justify designing for girls' rosters, not enough to size the buy.

Inseam direction is unresolved across the whole base and this opportunity takes a position (7"/9"/11") without settling it. One reading has performance consolidating at 6-7" and lifestyle at 9"+; the auditor's third position is the best-evidenced and cuts against both - Nike ships a continuous, fully merchandised 6/8/10/11" ladder with the LONGEST inseam at the LOWEST price (~$37), which is the opposite of a premium short-inseam architecture. For a competition bottoms system the rule constrains the answer (knee-clearing), so this contradiction is less damaging here than elsewhere in the portfolio - but the 11" coverage option is being priced as a mid-tier piece in a line where 11" is currently the basement, and that repositioning is unproven.

confidence_rationale: 52 reflects an unusually wide spread between the quality of the enabling FACT and the quality of everything needed to turn it into a business. WHAT IS SOLID (pushing up): the rulebook language is primary, dated and independently re-verified by me this session, and it does exactly what the thesis says - it makes a mixed-style, like-coloured roster order legal without a permission request (A06-S3). The biomechanics that specify the waistband and hem interface are the best-evidenced item in the entire base and survived their skeptic untouched (A06-S1). The channel direction is confirmed by audited financials on both sides - Nike wholesale +6% against Direct -6%, Digital down ten straight quarters (A04-S1, A02-S7). Australia is the best-verified non-US market signal in the base with every correction running in its favour (A02-S9). There is a countable addressable base: 896,944 US high-school basketball participants in 2024-25. And the competitive check I ran is genuinely encouraging - the colour-matched team tight is currently supplied by small custom-sublimation dealers at $41.99 with 8-unit minimums, which is a soft incumbent for a brand with a stock colour library. WHAT IS WEAK (pulling down hard): I broke the opportunity's own why-now - the rule is from 2023-24, not 2025-26, so three ordering cycles have already passed without a brand response. The layering prevalence that justifies the tight SKUs is entirely unmeasured below elite level. The channel signal contains no basketball-shorts data at all and its revenue base is contradicted. Core organised youth participation growth is contested in the US and negative in England. The women's waist-control feature rests on sizing boilerplate. And there is no shorts-level unit, price or sell-through data anywhere in this base, in any geography - no price here is anchored to a retrieved Nike price file. I did not go lower because the failure modes are cheap and fast to test: a broadcast-coding study of tights prevalence at sub-elite level, a count of the BSN catalogue, and one conversation with Nike Team Sports about bookings would resolve most of it inside a quarter. I did not go higher because at present this is a well-reasoned architecture with a verified legal opening and an unmeasured market.
what_would_need_to_be_true: Sub-elite layering prevalence is material. Coded observation of broadcast and recorded footage across a sample of US high-school, AAU/club and NCAA games, counting tights-wearing by length (3/4, full, none) and by gender, must show enough of a roster layering to justify a colour-matched tight as a stock SKU. A plausible go threshold is 20%+ of players on a typical roster; below roughly 10% the tight SKUs die and this becomes a short-only story. This single study either licenses or kills the opportunity and nothing else should be commissioned first.

Mixed-bottom rosters actually happen. A survey of 200+ high-school and club coaches and ADs across at least 8 states, three seasons after Rule 3-4-5 took effect, must establish (a) how many programmes currently have at least one athlete in a non-standard bottom, (b) how they solve it today, and (c) whether they would order a mixed set if it were on the dealer form at the prices above. Three cycles of silence is the central risk and this is the direct test of it.

Nike can hold the colour. Production-fabric colour trials across the knit short body and the elastane-rich compression construction must hit the stated tolerance (target dE <=1.0) in every colour in the library, repeatably, across sourcing countries. 'Like-coloured' is enforced by an official's eye at the table; if the tight reads as a different royal blue from the short, the programme has no product.

The team channel is genuinely low-markdown for basketball bottoms specifically. Nike Team Sports must produce bookings, fill rate, reorder frequency and realised markdown for basketball bottoms through BSN and peer dealers for FY24-FY26. If the team-channel markdown rate is not materially better than the wholesale rate, the margin case - which is the entire commercial thesis - disappears.

The FIBA length allowance for compression undershorts is real. The current FIBA rulebook and Official Interpretations must be read at source to confirm whether the 'any length' allowance covers undershorts or only undershirts, before any FIBA-legal claim is printed on a spec sheet or dealer catalogue.

The linerless short does not cannibalise more margin than it earns. If the lined short must remain in the line (it must - non-layering players need it), the SKU count rises rather than falls and the liner deletion funds nothing. Costed both ways, the system must still clear the team-channel margin hurdle at $32-38 net.

Girls' and club programmes actually reorder. Size-curve fill and rebuy rate by door for women's/girls' team bottoms must show replenishment behaviour, not one-time buys. A bookings franchise lives on reorder; a one-season buy at these prices does not pay for a colour library.

The compliance claim survives legal and standards review in every market it ships to, including the EU Empowering Consumers Directive regime that applies from 27 September 2026 for any environmental or performance claim on the hangtag or spec sheet.
what_we_still_dont_know: How many US high-school and club programmes currently have at least one athlete in a non-standard uniform bottom, and what they do about it today. Nobody in this base has counted, and three seasons of data now exist to count.

The size of the team-dealer basketball-bottoms pool in units or dollars. A04-S9 contains no basketball-shorts data of any kind; the $75M club/select figure and the $5B segment size could not be corroborated in any source; and Varsity's own revenue base is contradicted between $2.3B and ~$2.7B.
Layering prevalence at high-school, club and college level, by gender and by length. Not contested - entirely unmeasured. This is the binding unknown for the whole system.

What adidas, Under Armour and the custom-sublimation dealers already offer on the same order form. The BSN and adidas team catalogues are published and were never audited; the assumption that Nike's existing team basketball bottom is competitively weak is asserted with zero evidence and is trivially checkable.
Nike's own realised ASP, markdown rate and reorder frequency on basketball bottoms through the team channel. No price in this analysis is anchored to a retrieved Nike price file, in any geography.

Whether a mixed-bottoms roster is culturally acceptable to coaches and officials in practice, as opposed to legal on paper. Legality is not adoption; an official's eye and a coach's preference for uniformity are both real frictions that no evidence here addresses.

Whether the same architecture is legal and orderable outside the US. Australia, England and European federations follow FIBA, whose colour-match rule is confirmed but whose multiple-styles position is not, and France's hijab ban makes the modest-dress use case a non-market for federated play there.

Whether the coverage and modest-dress population is large enough to matter commercially. The need is credible and sustained; it has never been sized in any market, and the incumbent serving it (Asiya) has operated for a decade at a scale nobody has measured.
nike_right_to_win: Four things Nike has that a custom-sublimation dealer, a modest-sport specialist and a retreating competitor do not. (1) COLOUR AT SCALE. The product is a colour standard held across two different knit constructions in twelve colourways, repeatably, across sourcing countries - which is a materials, dye-house and QC capability, not a design idea. It is precisely the kind of unglamorous industrial problem Nike's scale solves and a $42-a-piece sublimation shop cannot. (2) THE ORDER FORM ALREADY EXISTS. Nike Team Sports is already distributed through BSN Sports alongside adidas, Under Armour, Puma and Lululemon (A04-S9); this programme adds SKUs to a catalogue Nike is already in, rather than building a channel. The competitive check is favourable: the colour-matched team tight today comes from small custom dealers at $41.99 with 8-unit minimums and artwork lead times, which a stock library beats on price, minimum and speed simultaneously. (3) ATHLETE EQUITY WITH THE EXACT END WEARER. Sabrina Ionescu, A'ja Wilson and Caitlin Clark are named by a retailer CEO on his own earnings call as what is driving basketball back, with boys and girls both buying (A04-S5) - and this programme reaches the girls' roster through her coach, which is a cheaper route to a consumer whose Nike mindshare is measurably falling (A01-S1) than brand marketing is. (4) THE COMPLIANCE CLAIM IS CERTIFIABLE. Knee-clearing across the full size grade, colour tolerance, logo placement and a wash-tested seam and shrinkage spec are all things Nike can measure and print, and they are exactly what a bookings buyer needs to justify a rebuy. HONEST COUNTERWEIGHTS: Nike does not disclose basketball apparel anywhere, so nobody inside this analysis can see whether Nike is currently strong or weak in this channel; Varsity/BSN is consolidating under a KKR-backed buyer, which strengthens the counterparty rather than Nike; and Nike's competitive advantage here is industrial rather than emotional, which means it will not defend itself in a line review against a product with a better image.

narrative:
I built this spec backwards from the only thing in the evidence base that is primary, dated and enforceable: a rulebook. Everything else here is a market read, a review corpus or a syndicated forecast, and most of it was shredded by its own skeptic. FIBA requires every player's compression garments - undershirts and undershorts - to be the same solid colour team-wide, and NFHS requires uniform bottoms to be like-coloured while permitting teammates to wear different STYLES. Read as a product brief rather than as officiating trivia, those two sentences say something no specialist said: the competition bottom is not a garment, it is a colour standard with four expressions, and the coach ordering it is buying compliance, not style.

The first judgement call was what to leave out. I stripped pockets, UPF, abrasion panels and cooling: pockets belong to the free-play family, UPF is close to free on polyester dry and unverified wet, abrasion is an outdoor problem. Every feature has to be defensible to a coach reading a dealer catalogue, and 'it matches, it is legal, it clears the knee in every size, and it survives twenty washes' is a complete argument for that reader.

The second call was the linerless short, and I argued with myself and lost. The synthesis treats liner deletion as a cost saving that funds the seam-and-shrinkage fix. It is not. Players who do not layer still need a liner, so the linerless short is an ADDITIONAL SKU in a programme whose whole pitch is a simple order form. I kept it, because a short sliding on slick compression across roughly 450 lateral movements a game is a design defect rather than a nuisance - but I removed the funding claim and flagged it as the most likely place the P&L breaks.

The third call changes the recommendation. The why-now was wrong, and I found it by checking. The synthesis dates NFHS Rule 3-4-5 to 2025-26; two independent sources put it in 2023-24, announced 15 May 2023. What actually changed for 2025-26 was the undershirt colour rule and the school logo rule. 3-4-5 appears in 2025-26 state summaries under 'New AND RECENT', which is almost certainly how it entered this base as current. The urgency argument is therefore gone, and a harder question replaces it: the permission barrier has been down for three ordering cycles and no brand appears to have stocked against it. That is either genuine whitespace or the market answering, and I could not tell from this evidence base. So I went to find the incumbent instead - and the incumbent is custom-sublimation micro-dealers charging USD 41.99 a piece with eight-unit minimums. That is a soft defence, and it is the most encouraging competitive fact in the file.

What I refused to do was claim a women's category gap. Three specialists tried it and three skeptics killed it; Nike ships 5", 6.5", 7" and 9" women's bottoms and put Aero-FIT on a women's signature short first. So this opportunity delivers coverage, waist control and extended sizes as COMPLIANCE, on a coach's order form, rather than as a category argument nobody can substantiate. That framing survives its own contradictions; the alternative did not.

One caution for the Council. This produces no image. It is a colour library, an order form and a wash test. It will lose a line review to anything with a hero shot, and it has to be judged on reorder rate and roster completeness instead - which means the decision to fund it must be made before it is ever presented visually.
